chapter_theme: Spring comes to Rajamapuram, and the whole city, likened to the Jina's walled assembly, pours out with litters, elephants, liquor, perfumes and powders to the water-play in the riverside groves; the women screen off a place in the grove, and Suramanjari and Gunamalai sit together until one holds out her powder, the start of the rivalry that opens the section.

cast.role: the god of love, lord of the five arrows, who brings spring
the women of Rajamapuram at the festival
a merchant's daughter of Rajamapuram, Gunamalai's rival in the powder contest
a merchant's daughter of Rajamapuram, Suramanjari's rival in the powder contest

851.reading: When the sun, in a stainless sky like the minds of gods who excel in faultless renunciation, has turned to the northern course, the lord of the five arrows arrives and makes the season of Panguni that ends the longing of the war camp.
851.event: Spring (Panguni) comes, brought by the god of love.
851.nuance: The section of a new marriage opens by likening the clear spring sky to the minds of renunciant gods: the season of desire is measured by the purity of those who have left it. பாசறைப் பரிவு may mean the war camp's hardship or the longing of those parted by it; the reading takes the second.

852.reading: Flower-laden branches are like women wearing ear ornaments and the bees reach them like men; swaying in the wind the branches bend like sulking women, and the thumbi, like the go-between who ends a sulk, embraces them from behind.
852.nuance: The whole grove is cast as a scene of lovers' sulking and reconciliation, with a third party, the சேடர், ending the quarrel: the poem stages oodal before the women of the story arrive.

853.reading: The forest, fragrant like the bodies of brides bathed in perfumed oil and scented with eaglewood, received the spring god as a guest.
853.nuance: Spring is வேனிலான், a person, and the forest plays the bride's household welcoming a guest (விருந்து).

854.reading: With the cuckoo calling from the branches and the thumbi and bees playing the yazh over the bathing pools, the spring that longs with burning desire came and settled in the heights.
854.nuance: Line 4 (தும்பர் நீடுறக் கத்தியல் பொத்ததே) is obscure as divided; the reading of spring taking its place is a guess.

855.reading: The people of Rajamapuram, a city fragrant with fresh naga flowers and given wholly to pleasure, went for their enjoyment to the flowering groves beside the river.
855.event: The people of Rajamapuram go out to the riverside groves for the spring festival.

856.reading: Wanting the festival's water-play, the old city whose drums never sleep rose up and went out, like the ancient walled precinct of the faultless lord of kevala appearing for worship.
856.event: The whole city sets out for the festival of water-play.
856.nuance: The simile is Jain: கேவலக் கிழவன் is the Jina possessed of kevala, perfect knowledge, and his மூதெயில் the walled assembly where he is worshipped. A pleasure festival is likened to the gathering round the Jina. தொழுவில் is taken as 'for worship'; it could be read otherwise.

857.reading: The sandal paste that women with water-vessels rubbed on with their palms and scattered turned the ground to slush, the elephants slipped, and the conches in the flood of water roared.
857.event: Women scatter sandal paste in the water-play until elephants slip on the ground.

858.reading: Pearl-hung litters that seem to swim, curtained carts, gold palanquins glowing in the young sun, fine young elephants and herds of she-elephants with garlanded riders go out.
858.event: The city's conveyances move out toward the grove.
858.nuance: The line ends in a list with no verb; the poem lets the procession of vehicles stand as a catalogue.

859.reading: The cries of those calling 'mount, help them mount', the shouts, the ear ornaments that slip and fall, and the ring of anklets on the road combine like a roaring great sea.

860.reading: The golden-shafted parasols, white umbrellas and peacock-feather fans crowd so that their light wanders as if at a loss, and the great city seems to have left its own circuit.
860.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (என்செய் கோவென் றிரிந்த திழைநிலா) are hard as divided; the moonlight of jewels 'wondering what to do' is a reading.

861.reading: The waving chowries are like the broken waves of the clear sea, the eaglewood smoke like twisted garlands, and the spreading pollen like a canopy stretched across the sky.

862.reading: Among the litters and carts, which are like waterfalls in the groves round a hill, the curtained elephants go like ranks of dark clouds.

863.reading: Baskets of Vanga and Kalinga silk, jewel caskets for the men, poles slung with strong liquor, and garlands at every turn are carried in haste.
863.event: The people hurry to the grove carrying silks, jewels, liquor and garlands.

864.reading: Carrying scented butter, sandal paste that bees swarm on, bathing powder, food to eat and baskets of faultless pleasures, the great crowd pours into the gateway of the grove.
864.event: The crowd enters the grove with its provisions.
864.nuance: The bathing powder (சுண்ணம்) appears here among the stores; it becomes the object of the quarrel that starts the section's story.

865.reading: The sounds of song, of tuned music, of dancing, of shouting and of plated elephants trumpeting rise through and reach the high sky.

866.reading: As though the golden heaven where the gods had played in flower-water had split the sky and dropped down whole as a great city, the sea-flood of people poured in there.
866.event: The crowd floods into the grove.

867.reading: Because the grove cooled the heat of the women with flashing sword-like eyes and warm breasts, they reached that grove of fresh flowers with no weariness at all.
867.event: The women arrive at the flowering grove.
867.nuance: The verse plays on வாட்டம் (withering, weariness) four times.

868.reading: On one side are pools crowded with lilies, stretches of water full of honeyed red lilies, and groves bright with fruit and birds.

869.reading: On another side are red-skinned plantains, branches dripping honey, mangoes and jackfruit with long fleshy pods, all ripe.

870.reading: Thieving monkeys, young black monkeys, leaping deer, herds of elephants, white swans and peacocks crowd the place and draw in the minds of those who look.

871.reading: With the women whose eyes are like spears enjoying the grove, the great lotus pools seem as if a mass of lotuses had fallen into the grove.
871.nuance: The text carries a stray dash in line 2 and the construction is hard; the reading that the women's faces among the trees are like lotuses fallen there is a guess.

872.reading: The flowering grove so described, oozing honey and fragrant, with white sand under its shade, seemed as if it had gone down into a clear pond.
872.nuance: The image of the grove 'entering a clear pool' is obscure as divided; the reading is tentative.

873.reading: In the grove they ringed a space with curtain screens and, entering it like the women of the gods with their mynahs and parrots chattering, sat down in their fine silks.
873.event: The women screen off a space in the grove and settle there.

874.reading: There Suramanjari, like a coral creeper of the sea, with jasmine in her hair, sat free of care with Gunamalai of the kovvai-red lips, and said this.
874.event: Suramanjari, seated with Gunamalai in the grove, begins to speak.
874.nuance: The two sit together எவ்வம் தீர்ந்து, without grief, just before their powders set them against each other.

875.reading: She of the silk-clad waist scented with incense smoke, of the large garlanded spear-like eyes and the fair forehead bearing its mark, held out her bright powder that bears desire.
875.event: One of the two women holds out her scented powder.
875.nuance: 874 ends with இது கூறினாள், but this verse describes, not speaks; the woman is named only by epithets. The reading takes her as Suramanjari, the one who has just begun to speak, but she may be Gunamalai or a maid.

links.note: The patikam tells that at the festival bath two young women quarrelled over their powders and swore not to bathe if they lost; here the two, Suramanjari and Gunamalai, sit together in the grove free of grief.
links.teaches: The patikam's quarrel is set against this calm first sight of the rivals side by side, so the story's discord grows out of an easy companionship and the festival's own luxury.

links.note: The powder is first held out here; the patikam says Suramanjari's powder was beaten and she withdrew vowing to look on no man.
links.teaches: A trifle of pleasure called the powder that bears desire becomes the cause of a vow against all men, so the section's marriage turns on a toiletry rather than a battle.

links.note: Paripadal 12 has Madurai dress, perfume itself and mount she-elephants, horses and chariots in a rush to meet the Vaiyai flood; the Cintamani's city sets out with litters, elephants and carts for its spring water-play by the river.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the Sangam river festival's order of dressing, mounting and rushing to the bank, but its festival honours no river or god, and is likened instead to the Jina's assembly, so the old civic rite is re-made as pure pleasure under a renouncer's image.

gains.a: a precedent showing that its procession is a set piece of the Tamil river festival rather than an invention
gains.b: evidence that its catalogue of the crowd's preparations survived as a convention into the later Jain epic, cut loose from the river's worship

links.note: The Cintamani calls the Jina the lord of faultless kevala; Tirumular calls kevala the soul's sleep of utter stupor under anava, from which karma drives it out.
links.teaches: The same word for the soul's state 'alone' is the summit of release for the Jain poet and the lowest darkness of the bound soul for the Saiva, so the two traditions disagree on whether the soul left to itself is free or blind.

gains.a: a sense of how pointed its epithet is: kevala names perfection only in a doctrine where the soul alone, freed of karma, is omniscient
gains.b: a rival use of its technical term, showing that its claim that the solitary soul is in darkness answers a school that called that solitude release

new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: விழவு நீர்விளை யாட்டு (856, line 2)

new_concepts.gloss: play and bathing in a river flood, as a festival of the town and a setting for lovers
new_concepts.label_source: the label is the house's; the verse says நீர்விளை யாட்டு (856, line 2)

source_issues: 851 line 2 (வடதிசை யயண ழன்னி) is garbled as written; the sense of the sun turning to its northern course (அயனம்) is a reading.
871 line 2 carries a stray dash (நுகர் - வேய்தலிற்) and the line is hard to construe.
852 line 2 has a full stop inside the verse (கொல்கி.); 863 lacks the final stop the other verses have.
860 lines 3-4 and 872 lines 2-4 are obscure as divided.
